extracted.intended_audience: General readers and stakeholders (claimants, lawyers, policymakers, public-health professionals) interested in asbestos law, compensation, health, and remediation
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic summary of legal, regulatory, medical, and compensation standards and practices relating to asbestos exposure, litigation, abatement, and trust-based compensation schemes across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust compensation categories (ARD1–ARD4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trust provides compensation for people in four categories related to Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARD): (ARD1) asbestosis / pleural thickening with mild to moderate; (ARD2) lung function impairment or with severe lung function impairment; (ARD3) asbestos-related lung cancer; (ARD4) mesothelioma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists the ARD category definitions and states average compensation since 2003 has been about R40,000 (ARD1), R80,000 (ARD2), R170,000 (ARD3) and R350,000 (ARD4). These amounts are paid over and above any compensation claimants might receive under the Occupational Diseases in Mines and Works Act (ODMWA).

rubrics_metrics.name: ART eligibility criteria for compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a case to be compensable under the Asbestos Relief Trust (ART), a victim needs to show that he/she was both exposed to asbestos from one of the operations run by the funders of the ART and has a compensable disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ART settlement was open and made provision for compensation to any person who met the compensation criteria set out in the Trust deed until the year 2028. (Practical implication: claimants must prove exposure traceable to funders’ operations plus clinical/diagnostic entitlement under Trust rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: ART claims projections and success-rate estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: ART modelling initially estimated about 16,800 individuals would submit claims, of whom approximately 5,036 (about 30%) would be successful; later revised to 5,162 successful claims with breakdowns (e.g., ~4.2% environmental claimants, ~2.9% lung cancer, ~10.8% mesothelioma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These projected numbers and success rates are used for trust funding and planning; the page notes some ratios (e.g., ARD1/ARD2) were not definitively estimated. (Use: actuarial estimation of liabilities and resource allocation for a compensation trust.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to prove exposure from funders' operations and disease causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensability requires demonstration both of exposure to asbestos originating from one of the funders’ operations and that the claimant has a compensable disease (per Trust deed criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a two-part evidentiary standard — source-of-exposure link and medical diagnosis — used by the ART and similar schemes; failure on either element defeats compensation under the Trust scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean Air Act asbestos-removal work-practice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clean Air Act requires that asbestos be wetted during removal and strictly contained, and that workers wear safety gear and masks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes federal prosecution of violations where contractors failed to wet/contain asbestos or protect workers. Work-practice rules have been treated as the basis for criminal or civil enforcement and are central to safe abatement standards (wetting, containment, PPE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for unsafe abatement and exploitative removal practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly removing asbestos improperly or exploiting vulnerable workers in illegal asbestos removal operations can give rise to criminal charges (e.g., violations of the Clean Air Act, RICO, obstruction, wire fraud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by indictments/convictions (e.g., Adamo Wrecking Company, RICO prosecutions, longest federal jail sentences for environmental crimes). The page highlights prosecutions using RICO and other statutes where removal was performed illegally or exploited homeless/undocumented workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: USEPA reporting requirement (1988) for asbestos in products
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1988 the United States Environmental Protection Agency issued regulations requiring certain U.S. companies to report the asbestos used in their products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulatory reporting obligation (and associated statutes such as 15 U.S. Code § 2607 on reporting/retention) is a compliance requirement intended to increase transparency about asbestos content in commerce and support enforcement and public-health responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy trusts as a compensation mechanism and their practical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When asbestos manufacturers file for bankruptcy they are typically required to fund special 'bankruptcy trusts' that pay reduced amounts to injured parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes these trusts pay 'pennies on the dollar' compared with tort recoveries but permit larger numbers of claimants to receive some compensation. (Implication for claimants: potentially faster but smaller recoveries; for policymakers: trade-offs between aggregate payout and number of claimants assisted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status of pleural plaques in the UK (test case and appellate reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2005 test-case ruling allowed compensation for pleural plaques, but that decision was reversed by the Court of Appeal and confirmed by the House of Lords in 2007; pleural plaques no longer constitute actionable injury in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, while Scotland preserved actionable status by legislation in 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records competing positions (insurers calling plaques 'simply a marker for asbestos exposure' vs. claimants calling the ruling a victory). This illustrates jurisdictional variance in what constitutes 'actionable injury' for asbestos-related conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment rule (House of Lords 2006) and legislative response (Compensation Act 2006)
rubrics_metrics.description: In May 2006 the House of Lords ruled that compensation for asbestos injuries should be reduced where responsibility could not be attached to a single employer; this was criticized and subsequently overturned by section three of the Compensation Act 2006.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a legal standard about apportioning liability among employers and the legislative power to modify judicially developed rules when perceived as unfair. (Practical lesson: statutory intervention can alter court-developed liability rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness standard for settlement classes and future claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Supreme Court rejected two large class-action settlements (1997 and 1999) because they would exclude future claimants or those who later developed asbestos-related illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a fairness/adequacy standard for mass settlements: settlements that preclude or unfairly restrict rights of future claimants are vulnerable to rejection by courts. (Relevant to design of global settlements and trust schemes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic standards and claimant eligibility controversy (ATS consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the proposed 'Fairness in Asbestos Injury Resolution Act of 2005' included that its approach to diagnosis was 'not consistent with the diagnostic criteria established by the American Thoracic Society' and therefore risked unfair exclusion of many ill people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites expert testimony urging that statutory or administrative eligibility criteria for compensation align with established medical diagnostic standards (e.g., ATS) to avoid exclusionary rules that contradict clinical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO position on chrysotile and asbestos carcinogenicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The World Health Organization recognizes that exposure to all types of asbestos fibers, including chrysotile, can cause cancer of the lung, larynx, and ovary, mesothelioma, and asbestosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a public‑health/medical standard undermining defendant arguments that chrysotile is less harmful; it is authoritative guidance used in regulatory, litigation, and policy contexts to assess hazard and causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defendant categories and liability theories in U.S. asbestos litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Asbestos lawsuits in the U.S. have included as defendants: manufacturers of machinery alleged to have required asbestos-containing parts, premises owners, banks that financed buildings/ships, retailers of asbestos-containing products, corporations alleged to have conspired to conceal dangers, manufacturers of tools used to cut/shaped asbestos parts, and manufacturers of respiratory protective equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page also notes common defense theories (e.g., that defendants did not ship asbestos-containing parts or only third parties installed them) and state-court rulings (e.g., Washington and California supreme courts deciding in favor of the defense on third-party part issues). This delineates how liability is framed and contested across product, premises, and conspiracy theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: International/national bans and prohibitions on asbestos use
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple jurisdictions have enacted laws/prohibitions banning asbestos or asbestos-containing products (examples cited include South Africa banning all use in 2008, Sweden banning use since 1982, and various national/regulatory instruments referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists legislative/regulatory actions and international instruments (e.g., Rotterdam Convention review) as policy standards for prohibition and control; practical implication: regulatory environments vary and inform removal, remediation, and trade rules.
